title: Forecast for the week of Nov 9
summary: I think this week turns on Tuesday's CPI, and the AI hardware selloff isn't finished. I expect the S&P to chop around its 200-day near 7,322, and I'd sell bounces into 7,500 to 7,600. I want equal weight to beat SPY and health care to beat tech again. MU should hold $600, but I don't think it gets back over its 200-day near $754 this week.
view:
Writing this Sunday evening. Last week the S&P fell 2.68% to 7,376.86, the Nasdaq fell 3.37% to 24,579.42, the Dow fell 0.94% to 51,285.73 and the Russell 2000 fell 2.05% to 2,754.11. Thursday did the damage: the S&P fell 4.4% and the Nasdaq 5.5% after reports that Microsoft would not expand a Texas data center deal with Nscale, on top of Democrats calling for a data center moratorium. Communication services (XLC +4.89%), real estate (XLRE +1.92%) and discretionary (XLY +1.91%) led. Energy (XLE -12.00%) and tech (XLK -8.23%) were worst, and the SOX fell 12.15%. The VIX went from 19.4 to 25.64, the 10-year closed at 4.86%, and Brent fell about 16% to $98.32. MU fell 22.0% on the week, from $884.74 to $690.00, including a 17.46% drop on Thursday.

This week hinges on inflation and the AI money trail. Payrolls came in at 165K against forecasts of 65K to 70K, unemployment fell to 4.1%, and CME odds of a December 9 hike rose to 76.8% from 66.9% a week earlier. CPI is Tuesday at 7:30 a.m. Sask, with 0.3% expected for headline (0.6% prior) and 0.2% for core (0.3% prior). There is no yearly headline rate this time because of the missing October 2025 data. PPI comes Friday. CoreWeave reports Tuesday after the close with about a 21% move priced, and Cisco (8.70%) and Applied Materials (14.37%) report Thursday after the close. Over the weekend, Nvidia's board opened an investigation into Jensen Huang, and Microsoft is winding down an Oracle AI cloud deal. Futures opened lower Sunday night, with the S&P down 0.4% and the Nasdaq 100 down 0.8%.

Last week taught me that the rankings work and tight lines don't. RSP over SPY and XLV over XLK both hit. Lines only 1% to 4% from the last close all broke. So I keep the two rankings and set the lines wider this time. The S&P cap at 7,600 is 3% above Friday's close, the 7,225 floor is scored only on the weekly close, and the MU floor at $600 is 13% below.

My lean is neutral, with the risk to the downside in AI hardware. Schwab reads the break of 7,600 as a completed double top that points to the 200-day near 7,300, and we are almost there. A hot CPI could push the S&P through 7,225. A soft one probably brings a bounce that stalls between 7,500 and 7,600. The risk to my calls is a soft CPI plus a good Applied Materials report setting off a chip squeeze, which would flip both rankings at once.

title: Forecast for the week of Nov 2
summary: I think this is a choppy week, and money is still moving out of the big tech names. I'd sell into tech bounces like today's until the S&P closes back over 7,632. I want equal weight to beat SPY and health care to beat tech, and I think the VIX falls once the election and Friday's jobs report are out of the way. MU should hold $800, but I'm not buying it until it gets back over $900.
view:
Writing this Tuesday morning, Election Day. Last week the S&P fell 0.57% to 7,580.07, the Nasdaq fell 2.00% and the Dow fell 0.85%, but the Russell 2000 rose 1.29% to 2,811.84. Health care (XLV +3.12%) and materials (XLB +2.79%) led. Communication services (XLC -5.32%) and tech (XLK -2.03%) were the only sectors down. Friday was the S&P's worst day since June: Intel fell 28.58% on its guidance and the SOX fell 7.20%. The VIX finished the week at 19.42, the 10-year at about 4.92%, and front-month Brent settled at $113.43. MU rose 0.8% on the week to $884.74.

Monday kept the rotation going. The S&P fell 0.51% to 7,541.40, its lowest close since July 31, and the Nasdaq fell 1.07%. The Dow rose 0.41% and RSP rose 0.76%. Brent dropped 7.63% to $104.77 on talk of US-Iran diplomacy, so energy (-3.96%) fell along with tech (-2.95%). Oracle's $20 billion stock and bond sale brought back the worries about how AI spending gets paid for. MU fell 5.78% to $833.59 after Kioxia's cautious outlook, and the VIX closed at 21.15. This morning chips are bouncing: the S&P is up about 0.3%, the Nasdaq about 0.7%, and MU is near $859.

This week hinges on three things. The midterms come in tonight, and Kalshi had Democrats at 93.8% to win the House and 74% for the Senate. AMD reports after the close tonight with about an 8.95% move priced, and Qualcomm and Arm report Wednesday. Payrolls come out Friday. The consensus is 55K to 63K, against 29K last month, and December hike odds were 72% on Monday. My lean is that payrolls come in under consensus, since Continuum (50K) and KPMG (45K) both sit below it. A soft number helps bonds and equal weight more than megacap tech.

My lean is neutral on the index and bearish on AI hardware when it rallies. The last two entries taught me that rankings and thresholds that follow the trend hit, while range pins and implied-move caps missed. So my calls ride the rotation and give the lines room. The risk is that the RSP and XLV calls miss together if AMD sets off a real tech squeeze.

recap:
The week split into three parts. Monday and Tuesday were soft: the S&P 500 closed Nov 2 at 7,541.40 and about 7,569 on Tuesday. Democrats won Congress, oil collapsed (Brent 94.62 on Wednesday), and the Dow jumped about 3%. The S&P 500 closed Wednesday at 7,688.62, above the 7,632 line the forecast said would cap it. The VIX fell to 16.61.

Thursday wiped that out. The S&P 500 fell 4.4% to 7,353.73 and the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5% to 24,315. The VIX jumped to 28.18 and MU fell 17.46% to $656.39. Friday's payrolls came in at +165,000 against a consensus near 59,000. Stocks bounced a little (S&P 500 7,376.86, VIX 25.64, MU $690.00). The S&P 500 lost 2.7% on the week. RSP fell about 1.8% from Monday's close, versus about 2.2% for the S&P 500. XLV was flat while XLK fell about 5.4%.

The rotation calls (RSP over SPY, XLV over XLK) and the Brent cap worked. The MU floor, the S&P cap and the VIX call did not. Score: 3 hits, 0 partials, 3 misses.
ai:
The relative-performance calls were the strongest part of the forecast. Equal weight and health care both beat their rivals by a clear margin, and the Brent cap held with room to spare. Those calls followed the trend and did not depend on one exact level. The Brent call was also easy, since Brent started the week at 104.77 and fell from there.

The level calls failed because they were too tight for a week with an election, an AI-capex scare and a payrolls print. The MU $800 floor sat only 4% under Monday's close, and the stock fell 7% in one day. The S&P cap at 7,632 was broken on Wednesday, only about 1% above Monday's close. The VIX call leaned on a soft payrolls print, and the report was far stronger than consensus. The bear scenario named a drop toward MU $800 and S&P 7,500, and the real move was much larger. The forecast's size of move was too small, and the calls did not allow for a one-day shock.
lesson: Keep ranking calls like relative strength, and give single-day price floors and caps a wider cushion, or score them on the weekly close. In a high-VIX week with big events, a line only 1% to 4% away from the last close will probably break.

title: Forecast for the week of Oct 19
summary: I think this week is a bounce, then chop. Monday's tech rally looks like an oversold bounce, not a bottom, so I'm not chasing it. Defensives and energy should stay the stronger trend unless Meta's capex update on Wednesday reassures the market about AI spending. The S&P has a ceiling around 7,712 to 7,739, and a close under 7,567 would mean a deeper AI unwind.
view:
Writing this Monday afternoon. Last week was a rotation more than a crash. The S&P fell 1.95% to 7,659.44 and the Nasdaq fell 4.48%, while the Dow rose 0.67%. Staples (XLP +5.02%), energy (XLE +4.86%) and health care (XLV +3.45%) led, and tech (XLK -7.70%) and small caps (Russell 2000 about -3.0%) took the hit. The SOX fell 8 sessions in a row, about 15.7%.

Monday's rally is the bounce. The S&P is up about 0.65% near 7,709, the Nasdaq about 1.4%, and the VIX is down to about 18. But the S&P is still sitting on its 50-day (about 7,706 to 7,712), and sentiment was fearful but not panicked on Friday (VIX 19.99, Fear & Greed 30). I read that as a reflex rally, with a likely ceiling at 7,712 to 7,739.

This week is earnings, not the Fed. The Fed is in its blackout before the Oct 27-28 meeting, with about a 15% chance of an October hike priced and about 89% by December. The swing event is Meta and Tesla after the close Wednesday. Meta's 2026 capex guide is $130 to $145 billion and the options market is pricing a move of about 6%. IBM and Lam Research also report Wednesday.

My lean is neutral. Health care, staples and energy stay the higher-conviction leaders, small caps keep lagging while the 10-year sits near 5.1%, and Brent stays in the $100 to $110 range. If Meta reassures, tech can keep bouncing. If it doesn't, 7,567 is the line.

recap:
The bounce came first, as expected. The S&P rose Monday through Wednesday to 7,757.17, then the AI sell-off took over. Thursday it fell 1.21% to 7,663.43 with the Nasdaq down 2.6% and semis down more than 6%, and Friday it slipped again to 7,623.68. That left the S&P down about 0.5% on the week (7,659.44 on Oct 16).

Energy beat tech: XLE went from 68.24 to 69.33 (+1.6%) while XLK went from 183.47 to 183.23 (-0.1%). XLK was ahead midweek after Wednesday's jump to 188.54, then gave it all back on Thursday. Small caps did not lag. The Russell 2000 rose from 2,721.37 to about 2,776 (+2.0%) and held up through Thursday's sell-off, beating the S&P by about 2.5 points. Meta fell about 7% on Thursday after its report, more than the 6% move the call allowed. Brent never came close to $100: it settled near $108.8 to $109.6 Monday to Wednesday, $113.17 Thursday, and ran higher Friday on Middle East tensions.

Calls 1 and 4 are hits. Call 2 is a miss because the Russell beat the S&P by a wide margin. Call 3 is a miss by about a point. The general bearish AI row had no wrong-if, so it isn't scored, though AI names did lead the drop on Thursday. Score: 2 hits, 2 misses, or 2 out of 4.
ai:
What's good: three of the four calls are ranking or threshold calls with a clear wrong-if, which fits last week's lesson of fewer exact price pins. The two relative calls (energy over tech, small caps under the S&P) only need an order, so no price level has to hold.

What to watch: the energy call has an easy trap, because a single big tech bounce day can flip a weekly ranking, and last week's tech drop of 7.7% makes a snap-back more likely than usual. The Meta call is symmetric, so a calm reaction wins and a big move either way loses, and that is a coin-flip-sized bet. The Brent call has about a 7% cushion from the $107.6 Monday level to $100, so it is a lower bar than the others. No trades are listed, so this entry is a pure forecast.

The bearish AI row is a general lean with no level and no wrong-if, so it can't be graded as written. Turning it into a call with a wrong-if, such as an AI basket finishing the week behind the S&P, would let it count in the record.
lesson: The two calls that followed the strongest trend (energy over tech, oil over $100) both hit, and the two that bet on a size or a lag missed. Small caps had already turned before the week started, so a lagging call needed a fresh reason, not last week's pattern. For earnings, the options market's implied move is a typical size, not a cap; with AI names already under pressure, Meta's move ran past it.

recap:
Thursday played out like the base case. The S&P closed at 7,744.06 (+0.33%), above the 7,725 call wall, and the VIX was 16.46. PPI was the surprise: September came in at +1.3% m/m (6.3% y/y) against about 0.5-0.6% expected, and core was +0.7% against 0.3%. October hike odds went to roughly 27-29% after the print, with a December hike priced near 78%. SOX closed down 0.88% at 11,581.22, and MU rose 1.87% to $931.24 without trading above $931.65.

Friday played out like the bear case. The S&P fell 1.09% to 7,659.44, closing 3.56 points under the 7,663 flip. The VIX jumped 21.45% to 19.99, a penny under the line. SOX fell 3.83% to 11,137.29, its eighth straight decline, and MU dropped 5.63% to $878.84, under $900. October hike odds eased to about 15% after Warsh gave no hike signal.

Over the two days NVDA (-3.24%) beat MU (-3.86%), and Staples (+1.81%) and Health Care (+1.58%) beat Tech (XLK about -3.6%, with Friday's close estimated).

Call 1 is graded partial: SOX closed red and far under 12,200, so its wrong-if line held, but the closes don't show a morning bounce. Call 2 is a miss because PPI came in at more than double the forecast and a December hike was priced near 78%. Call 7 is a hit by one penny. Score: 3 hits, 1 partial, 3 misses, or 3.5 out of 7.
ai:
What's good: the wrong-if lines made this easy to grade. Most calls settled on one number, and the 7,663 line is clear, since the S&P closed 3.56 points under it. The two relative calls, NVDA over MU and Staples and Health Care over Tech, both held in a falling market, because they only needed a ranking and no price level had to hold.

What missed: the level calls. The S&P pin range and the MU range both assumed a calm market, and Friday's 1.09% drop broke both. The PPI call used the consensus figure as the forecast, so it carried no view of its own. A print of +1.3% against 0.5-0.6% expected misses for anyone who sat on consensus. A call on a data release only helps if it says which way the surprise leans and why.

What to watch: the warning that calls 3, 6 and 7 would miss together was half right. Call 3 missed with call 4 on Friday, but 6 and 7 held. The VIX hit is the thinnest grade here, since 19.99 sits a penny under the line after a 21% jump. The bear scenario had 25% odds and most of its markers (S&P under 7,663, VIX at 19-20, MU through $900) showed up Friday. A quarter looks light for a market that had just printed a hot CPI with semis already sliding. Seven calls is a small sample, so 3.5 out of 7 says little about skill yet.
